---
title: "Scientific Objecthood"
subtitle: "The boundary participates in defining what counts as the object"
toc: true
---

Science is organized around objects.

Physics has particles, fields, masses, charges, and spacetime.

Chemistry has atoms, molecules, and reactions.

Biology has proteins, cells, tissues, and organisms.

Other sciences define still other objects.

R<sup>2</sup>D begins with a question that comes before deciding which of
these objects is most fundamental:

> **What makes something a scientific object in the first place?**

Its answer is boundary relative.

> **An object is a readable state distinction defined at a count boundary.**

The boundary does not merely surround an independently existing object.

It participates in defining what counts as the object.

## From Objects to Objecthood

A conventional foundational question is:

> What are the fundamental objects of nature?

R<sup>2</sup>D asks a logically earlier question:

> What conditions must be satisfied before anything can count as an object?

Before an electron, molecule, protein, cell, or organism can be scientifically
identified, some differences must be readable.

Those differences must be classified relative to a count domain.

A boundary must therefore already define:

- which distinctions are readable;
- which realizations are compatible;
- which compatible realizations belong to the same state;
- and which differences count as changes of that state.

Objecthood begins with this classification architecture.

[Boundaries Define Scientific Objects →](boundaries.qmd)

## A Boundary Defines a State Domain

At boundary $B_n$, let

$$
\mathfrak M_n
$$

be the compatible formal microstate domain.

Let

$$
\mathcal M_n
$$

be the readable macrostate domain.

The boundary supplies the classification

$$
\boxed{
\pi_n:
\mathfrak M_n
\rightarrow
\mathcal M_n.
}
$$

A readable state

$$
i\in\mathcal M_n
$$

is therefore defined relative to that boundary.

Its multiplicity is

$$
\boxed{
W_{n,i}
=
\left|
\pi_n^{-1}(i)
\right|.
}
$$

The object is not added afterward to this structure.

The readable state classification is what makes the object scientifically
distinguishable there.

## A Scientific Object Is a Readable Distinction

R<sup>2</sup>D therefore uses a deliberately broad concept of objecthood.

An object need not be a small solid thing.

A scientific object can be any stable readable distinction defined by an
appropriate boundary.

Thus a particle can be an object.

A molecule can be an object.

A protein conformation can be an object.

A cell can be an object.

An organism can be an object.

The common requirement is not a shared substance.

It is a shared formal condition:

$$
\boxed{
\text{boundary}
\rightarrow
\text{readable distinction}
\rightarrow
\text{state identity}.
}
$$

## Objecthood Is Real

Boundary-relative objecthood does not mean that objects are illusions.

A molecule can be physically real.

A cell can be physically real.

A particle can be physically real.

Their properties can be measured.

Their transitions can be manipulated.

They can enter highly predictive causal models.

R<sup>2</sup>D does not require otherwise.

The restriction is narrower:

$$
\boxed{
\text{real at }B_n
\not\Rightarrow
\text{primitive at every boundary}.
}
$$

Thus:

> **Boundary-relative reality is still reality.**

## Reality and Primitiveness Are Different Claims

Suppose an object is experimentally readable at $B_n$.

That establishes its scientific reality relative to that boundary.

It does not automatically establish that the same identity survives as a
primitive object at

$$
B_{n+1}.
$$

R<sup>2</sup>D therefore separates:

$$
\boxed{
\text{scientific reality}
}
$$

from

$$
\boxed{
\text{boundary-independent primitiveness}.
}
$$

These are not equivalent claims.

This distinction allows familiar scientific objects to remain completely real
without requiring one privileged ontology to persist through all scales.

## The Primitive-Object Error

Suppose an object is a legitimate readable state distinction at $B_n$.

Now change the count boundary.

The old state identity may no longer remain readable as the same state at

$$
B_{n+1}.
$$

Its realization may instead contribute to the multiplicity of a newly
classified enclosing state.

If the subordinate identity is nevertheless assumed to remain independently
primitive, R<sup>2</sup>D calls this a **primitive-object projection**.

Schematically:

$$
\boxed{
\text{object at }B_n
\not\Rightarrow
\text{same primitive object at }B_{n+1}.
}
$$

The problem is not believing that the object exists.

The problem is assuming that its boundary-specific identity must persist
unchanged after the state classification has changed.

## Objecthood Changes With the Boundary

At $B_n$, an object may be represented by macrostate

$$
i_n.
$$

At $B_{n+1}$, that local identity can become part of a compatible formal
microstate realization:

$$
\mu_{n+1}.
$$

Thus the same recursively organized realization can change status:

$$
\boxed{
\text{macrostate meaning at }B_n
\rightarrow
\text{microstate meaning relative to }B_{n+1}.
}
$$

This is not merely a change in vocabulary.

It is a change in the count relation by which the object is defined.

[Macrostate and Microstate →](macrostate-microstate.qmd)

## A Coin Is Already Boundary Relative

A single coin provides the simplest example.

At one boundary, the readable states may be

$$
H
\qquad\text{and}\qquad
T.
$$

The coin is the scientific object.

Now place ten coins inside an ensemble boundary.

The readable object can instead be the ensemble state

$$
N_H=0,1,\ldots,10.
$$

At that boundary, the individual coin states participate in the realization
of the ensemble macrostate.

The scientifically readable object has changed.

The coins have not become unreal.

But the ensemble is not merely another name for one of them.

It has its own state domain and multiplicity.

[The Coins Example →](coins.qmd)

## A Component Is Also an Object — At Its Own Boundary

This avoids another common misunderstanding.

Calling something a component does not make it less real.

A myosin molecule is a legitimate object at a molecular boundary.

A protein is a legitimate object at a protein boundary.

A cell is a legitimate object at a cellular boundary.

But relative to a larger boundary, that same object may serve as one
subordinate realization among many.

Thus:

$$
\boxed{
\text{object}
\leftrightarrow
\text{component}
}
$$

is itself boundary dependent.

What is a whole at one boundary can participate as a component of another.

## Components Do Not Create the Multiplicity of the Whole

Suppose boundary $B_n$ defines macrostate $i$.

Its multiplicity is

$$
W_{n,i}
=
\left|
\pi_n^{-1}(i)
\right|.
$$

That cardinality is defined by the boundary classification.

A particular subordinate component realization can occupy one member of that
class.

It cannot create the cardinality of the class by occurring.

Therefore:

> **Components realize multiplicity structure.  
> They do not create multiplicity structure.**

This distinction is central to R<sup>2</sup>D objecthood.

The object defined at the enclosing boundary has a possible structure that is
not reducible to the history of one subordinate component.

[Multiplicity →](multiplicity.qmd)

## The Whole Is Not the Arithmetic Sum of Its Objects

Suppose many peer boundaries are jointly compatible.

Their possible realizations compose multiplicatively:

$$
W_{\mathrm{joint}}
=
\prod_\alpha W_\alpha.
$$

The enclosing boundary then classifies those compatible joint realizations
into its own readable macrostates.

Thus the whole-system object is not simply

$$
\text{object}_1
+
\text{object}_2
+
\cdots.
$$

Instead:

$$
\boxed{
\text{compatible peer realizations}
\rightarrow
\text{new enclosing classification}.
}
$$

The larger object exists through a new multiplicity structure.

## Persistence Does Not Require Persistent Parts

Boundary-relative objecthood also changes what it means for an object to
persist.

Suppose the classification defining an enclosing object remains stable while
its subordinate realizations change.

Then the object can remain identifiable even while its components are
replaced.

Thus:

$$
\boxed{
\text{persistent object identity}
\not\Rightarrow
\text{persistent subordinate identity}.
}
$$

This is common in organized systems.

A biological structure can persist while molecules turn over.

A cell can persist while proteins are synthesized and degraded.

An organism can persist while large numbers of its subordinate components
change.

Persistence belongs to the boundary-defined organization, not necessarily to
the permanent identity of every subordinate part.

## Object Persistence Is Recurrent Organization

What makes an object persist is therefore not simply possession of the same
matter at every occurrence.

More generally, persistence requires that the boundary continue to support
the distinctions by which the object is identified.

Schematically:

$$
\boxed{
\text{stable boundary classification}
+
\text{recurrent compatible realization}
\rightarrow
\text{persistent objecthood}.
}
$$

The particular subordinate realization can change.

The organizing relation can remain.

This gives R<sup>2</sup>D a natural account of objects whose components
continually turn over.

## Stability Does Not Make an Object Primitive

A long-lived object may appear especially fundamental.

But persistence does not establish boundary independence.

An object can remain stable for billions of local recurrences and still be
defined relative to a particular count domain.

Thus:

$$
\boxed{
\text{stability}
\not\Rightarrow
\text{primitiveness}.
}
$$

Stability tells us that a classification is recurrently realized.

It does not tell us that the classification exists independently of every
boundary.

## Change Can Occur Without Loss of Objecthood

An object also need not remain in one macrostate to remain the same
scientific object.

Its state may change:

$$
i
\rightarrow
k.
$$

What persists is the boundary-defined state domain within which both
macrostates belong to the same object classification.

Thus a muscle can shorten.

A protein can change conformation.

A cell can divide or differentiate.

An atom can change state.

Objecthood does not require absence of change.

It requires that the change remain readable within an organizing state
domain.

## Structural Change Can Redefine the Object

But sometimes the classification itself changes.

Suppose

$$
\pi_n
\rightarrow
\pi_n'.
$$

Then the state domain changes.

The previous object classification may no longer apply.

Thus:

$$
\boxed{
\text{parameter change}
\neq
\text{classification change}.
}
$$

A model can therefore fail not because one parameter drifted, but because the
scientific object itself has been redefined by a changed count boundary.

This distinction can be important in systems undergoing phase transitions,
developmental transitions, structural reorganization, or other changes in
what distinctions remain scientifically meaningful.

## Objecthood Is Not Mere Spatial Containment

A boundary in R<sup>2</sup>D is not necessarily a physical surface.

Therefore objecthood is not defined merely by drawing a geometric outline
around something.

A boundary is the relation that defines the count domain.

It determines which differences belong to the same state classification and
which do not.

Thus:

$$
\boxed{
\text{object boundary}
\neq
\text{necessarily geometric surface}.
}
$$

A spatial surface can later become one physical read of a boundary.

But boundary-defined objecthood comes first.

## Objecthood Comes Before Physical Geometry

This has an important consequence.

If a physical object must already be distinguishable before we can assign it a
position, radius, volume, or trajectory, then those spatial coordinates
cannot be logically prior to objecthood.

The order is

$$
\boxed{
\text{boundary-defined distinction}
\rightarrow
\text{object}
\rightarrow
\text{physical coordinate}.
}
$$

Not

$$
\text{pre-existing spatial coordinate}
\rightarrow
\text{object}.
$$

The later gravitational program develops this distinction much further.

[Why the Mathematics Comes Before Units →](before-units.qmd)

## Objecthood Comes Before Probability

The same argument applies statistically.

Before assigning a probability to an object being in state \(i\), the state
domain must already exist.

The boundary must already define

$$
\mathcal M_n.
$$

The compatible realizations must already define

$$
W_{n,i}.
$$

Only then can those counts be normalized into probability.

Thus:

$$
\boxed{
\text{object and state definition}
\rightarrow
\text{possible count}
\rightarrow
\text{probability}.
}
$$

Probability does not define the object whose states it normalizes.

## Objecthood Comes Before Energy

Likewise, assigning an energy

$$
E_i
$$

to state $i$ presupposes that state $i$ has already been distinguished.

So the logical order is

$$
\boxed{
\text{state distinction}
\rightarrow
\text{physical energy read}.
}
$$

R<sup>2</sup>D therefore begins before energetic ontology.

Part II asks how energetic quantities become physical readings of already
defined recursive count relations.

## Different Sciences Can Have Different Real Objects

If objecthood is boundary relative, then different sciences do not need to
share one privileged object vocabulary.

Physics can legitimately describe particles.

Chemistry can legitimately describe molecules.

Biology can legitimately describe cells and organisms.

The existence of one level does not make the others fictional.

Each domain can identify real objects defined by the distinctions readable
there.

Thus:

> **Boundary-relative objecthood permits scientific pluralism without
> abandoning formal unification.**

What changes across domains is the object.

What can remain invariant is the grammar by which an object is defined.

## Unification Does Not Require One Universal Object

This changes the usual unification problem.

A common strategy is to search for one final object from which every other
scientific object is built.

R<sup>2</sup>D proposes a different invariant.

Not:

$$
\boxed{
\text{one object at every scale}.
}
$$

But:

$$
\boxed{
\text{one formal architecture by which objects become distinguishable}.
}
$$

That architecture is

$$
\boxed{
\text{boundary}
\rightarrow
\text{distinction}
\rightarrow
\text{classification}
\rightarrow
\text{multiplicity}
\rightarrow
\text{realization}.
}
$$

The objects change.

The grammar need not.

## A Particle and an Organism Need Not Share an Ontology

This is why R<sup>2</sup>D does not need to claim that an organism is
"really" only a collection of particles in order to connect physics and
biology formally.

Nor does it need to claim that particles and organisms are the same kind of
physical object.

Their count domains differ.

Their readable states differ.

Their physical coordinates differ.

Yet both can instantiate the same primitive relation:

$$
\boxed{
\text{boundary-defined objecthood}.
}
$$

The unification occurs at the level of the grammar, not the domain-specific
object.

## Mechanism Does Not Define Objecthood

Once an object has been defined, one can ask how its state changes.

That is a mechanistic question.

A sequence of subordinate transitions may realize

$$
i\rightarrow k.
$$

Those events can be necessary.

They can be experimentally manipulable.

They can be legitimate effective causes.

But the mechanism does not, by itself, define the state domain within which

$$
i
$$

and

$$
k
$$

are distinguishable.

Thus:

$$
\boxed{
\text{mechanism}
\neq
\text{definition of the object}.
}
$$

Mechanism operates within an object architecture that must already be
specified.

## Effective Causes Can Be Real

Boundary-relative causality follows the same logic as boundary-relative
objecthood.

Suppose manipulating local variable $X$ changes readable outcome $Y$.

Then $X$ can legitimately be described as an effective cause within that
boundary.

R<sup>2</sup>D does not prohibit such causal language.

It asks a separate question:

> Does that local effective cause also define the enclosing organization under
> which the relation is realized?

Not necessarily.

Thus:

$$
\boxed{
\text{effective cause}
\not\Rightarrow
\text{primitive causal organizer}.
}
$$

[The Causal Inversion →](causal-inversion.qmd)

## Object, Interaction, and Organizing Structure

R<sup>2</sup>D identifies a common explanatory sequence.

First, a boundary-relative object is treated as primitive.

Then correlations among such objects are represented as primitive
object-object interactions.

Then a field, potential, geometry, wavefunction, or other organizing
structure may be introduced to organize those interactions.

Schematically,

$$
\boxed{
\text{recursive organization}
\rightarrow
\text{object}
\rightarrow
\text{interaction}
\rightarrow
\text{organizing field or geometry}.
}
$$

The resulting theories can be extraordinarily accurate.

R<sup>2</sup>D does not object to their mathematics.

It asks whether the projected objects and structures have been promoted too
far down the ontological hierarchy.

## Predictive Success Does Not Establish Primitive Objecthood

A theory written in terms of boundary-relative objects can be extremely
predictive.

That is expected.

Stable enclosing organization can generate stable local correlations.

A model of those correlations can therefore work exceptionally well.

Thus:

$$
\boxed{
\text{predictive success}
\not\Rightarrow
\text{primitive objecthood}.
}
$$

The equations may be right.

The question of what their variables are **fundamentally** remains separate.

## No View From No Boundary

If every readable object is boundary indexed, there is no scientifically
readable description from "no boundary."

Every measurement resolves some distinctions and not others.

Every state classification belongs to some count domain.

Science can compare boundaries.

It can move between them.

It can reconstruct recursive relations.

But a readable scientific object is always defined somewhere.

Thus:

> **There is no view from no boundary.**

This does not make science subjective.

The boundary is part of the formal definition of what is being measured.

## Boundary Relative Does Not Mean Observer Arbitrary

A boundary is also not merely whatever an observer chooses to imagine.

The proposed boundary must correctly identify:

- the readable distinctions;
- the compatible realization domain;
- the macrostate classification;
- the multiplicity structure;
- the observable transitions;
- and the enclosing relations organizing realization.

A poor boundary definition will fail empirically.

Boundary relativity therefore does not mean arbitrary relativity.

It means that scientific claims must be indexed to the count domain in which
their objects are defined.

## Scientific Truth Can Be Boundary Relative

A particle description can be true within the boundary where particles are
readable.

A thermodynamic description can be true where temperature, entropy, heat,
and work are readable.

A gravitational geometry can be true where that geometry is the appropriate
physical read.

These truths do not have to be false merely because R<sup>2</sup>D places
them downstream of a more primitive count architecture.

Thus:

$$
\boxed{
\text{boundary-relative truth}
\neq
\text{falsehood}.
}
$$

The stronger question is whether a boundary-relative scientific coordinate
should be promoted to universal primitive ontology.

## The Primitive Invariant Is Not the Object

This leads to the broadest interpretation of R<sup>2</sup>D.

The proposed invariant across science is not:

- one particle;
- one molecule;
- one force;
- one field;
- one organism;
- one geometry;
- or one universal ruler.

It is the architecture by which scientific objects become defined.

That architecture includes:

$$
\boxed{
\text{boundary}
}
$$

$$
\boxed{
\text{distinguishability}
}
$$

$$
\boxed{
\text{classification}
}
$$

$$
\boxed{
\text{multiplicity}
}
$$

$$
\boxed{
\text{occurrence}
}
$$

$$
\boxed{
\text{occupancy}
}
$$

$$
\boxed{
\text{recurrence}
}
$$

and

$$
\boxed{
\text{recursive replacement}.
}
$$

The object can change.

The architecture can remain.

## R<sup>2</sup>D as a Theory of Scientific Objecthood

This is why R<sup>2</sup>D is broader than a proposal about one physical
domain.

It does not primarily ask:

> What is an electron?

It asks:

> What makes an electron count as one scientific object?

It does not primarily ask:

> What is a protein?

It asks:

> What makes a protein a persistent readable state while its subordinate
> realization changes?

It does not primarily ask:

> What is an organism?

It asks:

> What defines the boundary within which an organism remains a scientific
> object despite continual component replacement?

And it does not begin by asking:

> What is spacetime?

It asks:

> What must already be distinguishable before a spatial or temporal
> coordinate can be assigned?

That is why the Canon describes R<sup>2</sup>D as a proposed theory of
**scientific objecthood and organization**.

## The Architecture in One View

Scientific objecthood can be summarized as

$$
\boxed{
\begin{array}{c}
B_n
\\[4pt]
\Downarrow
\\[4pt]
\text{readable distinctions}
\\[4pt]
\Downarrow
\\[4pt]
\mathcal M_n
\\[4pt]
\Downarrow
\\[4pt]
W_{n,i}
=
\left|\pi_n^{-1}(i)\right|
\\[4pt]
\Downarrow
\\[4pt]
\text{realized state}
\\[4pt]
\Downarrow
\\[4pt]
\text{scientific object at }B_n
\end{array}
}
$$

Changing the boundary gives

$$
\boxed{
B_n
\rightarrow
B_{n+1}
\quad\Rightarrow\quad
\text{new count domain}
\rightarrow
\text{new object classification}.
}
$$

So:

$$
\boxed{
\text{object at }B_n
\not\Rightarrow
\text{primitive object at }B_{n+1}.
}
$$

## The Key Distinction

The simplest summary is:

> **An object is real where it is distinguishable.**

> **Its identity is defined by the boundary that makes those distinctions
> countable.**

> **Its subordinate realizations can change while its organization
> persists.**

> **Its reality at one boundary does not require its identity to remain
> primitive at every other boundary.**

R<sup>2</sup>D therefore shifts the foundational question from

> **What is the fundamental object?**

to

> **What is the formal grammar by which anything becomes a scientific
> object?**

The next step is to recognize that this grammar has been defined without
meters, seconds, joules, kelvin, or any other physical unit.
